title: Pause, verify, then act
learningGoal: Recognize high-risk requests, distinguish appearance from evidence, and verify a contact independently.
pauseQuestion: For the two fictional contacts, identify the requested action, one warning cue, and the verification route. Pause before choosing.
workedExplanation: Do not transfer money or share a code. Independently contact the bank. For the possible CRA notice, navigate to Canada.ca yourself and verify the account notice; CRA may call, so do not use a blanket rule.

scenes.title: Two messages, two requests
scenes.visualDescription: Read the action—not just the logo.
onScreenLabels: A  “Move your money to our safe account. Send the code.”
B  “A new tax notice is available.”
scenes.formulaOrDecision: What does each contact want you to do?
scenes.narration: Two fictional contacts arrive. A bank-looking text says a transfer is at risk and asks the person to move money to a “safe account” and reply with a one-time code. A second notice says a tax message is waiting and tells the person to sign in through the usual government route. A familiar logo or official-sounding name does not identify the sender. Start by underlining the action each message requests and decide whether it is reversible or sensitive.

scenes.title: Spot pressure and sensitive requests
scenes.visualDescription: A cue raises concern; verify before acting.
onScreenLabels: Urgency or threat
Transfer to a “safe” account
One-time code or password
Remote access or unusual payment
scenes.formulaOrDecision: Cue ≠ proof • pause before an irreversible action.
scenes.narration: Scams often create urgency, secrecy, threats, or an unexpected reward. Requests to transfer money to a “safe account,” buy gift cards, use cryptocurrency, install remote-access software, or share a password or one-time code are high-risk. Poor spelling can be a clue, but polished writing does not prove a message is real. A cue is evidence to slow down, not a complete identity test. Do not click, reply, transfer, or share secrets while pressured.

scenes.title: Verify through a separate route
scenes.visualDescription: Do not use the contact path supplied by the suspicious message.
onScreenLabels: PAUSE
Find the official service independently
Ask if the request is real
Act only through a verified route
scenes.formulaOrDecision: Known app • saved statement • official website typed independently
scenes.narration: For a bank concern, open the known app or use contact details from a bank card or statement. Do not call a number included only in the unexpected text, and do not trust caller ID by itself. For a web notice, navigate to the known official site yourself rather than following a message link. If uncertain, talk to a trusted adult and ask the institution through an independently found route. A search result or advertisement may also be misleading; use the known official domain.

scenes.title: CRA contact needs a precise rule
scenes.visualDescription: CRA may contact people; caller ID is not proof.
onScreenLabels: CRA may call, write, or send notifications
Caller ID can be spoofed
Never share passwords or security codes
Ask, end, verify independently if unsure
scenes.formulaOrDecision: Use the CRA contact-verification tool or Canada.ca details.
scenes.narration: Do not memorize the false rule “CRA never calls.” The Canada Revenue Agency may contact people by phone and other channels. A caller ID that displays a government name still does not prove who is calling. If a person is unsure, they can ask for the caller’s name, office, and callback number, end the call, and check using CRA’s official contact-verification tool or contact details found independently on Canada.ca. CRA may request some information for a legitimate identity check or missing tax information, but never share passwords or one-time security codes with an unexpected caller.

scenes.title: Worked answer: safe without guessing
scenes.visualDescription: Verify the contact; do not make an irreversible move.
onScreenLabels: A  Do not transfer or share the code; contact the bank independently.
B  Navigate to Canada.ca yourself and check for the notice.
Unknown sender identity? Verify before acting.
scenes.narration: For message A, the safe-account transfer and code request are high-risk. Do not transfer or reply; contact the bank independently. For message B, the notification may be legitimate, but this fictional card is not proof. Navigate to Canada.ca yourself and check the account through the official route. If a caller claims to be CRA, remember that CRA can call, but caller ID can be spoofed. Ask for callback details, end the call, and verify independently if unsure. The lesson is neither “trust it” nor “all contacts are fake.” It is pause, verify, then act. If a learner already clicked or shared information, the response changes: stop interacting, secure the affected account from a trusted device, and promptly contact the relevant institution through an independently found route. Preserve the message and time, but do not reopen its link to collect evidence. If money was lost, contact local police promptly and report through current Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre guidance. Reporting does not guarantee recovery. A second person offering guaranteed reimbursement for an upfront fee is another reason to pause and verify.
